props.title: Enter the Void
props.initialSlug: A psychedelic journey through death and Tokyo's underworld

sections.content: Enter the Void (2009) revolutionized first-person perspective filmmaking through Gaspar Noé's hallucinatory vision of death and rebirth in Tokyo. Shot primarily from an overhead perspective or through the protagonist's eyes - even after death - it builds on the experimental foundations laid by Lady in the Lake (1947) while pushing technical boundaries that influenced later works like Hardcore Henry (2015). The film's neon-drenched psychedelic sequences and seamless digital transitions created a new visual language for depicting altered states, drawing from the DMT experiences described in The Spirit Molecule (2010) documentary. Climax|2018|Noé's dance horror film follows a troupe whose sangria gets spiked with LSD, descending into chaos filmed in long, swirling takes|Showtime Irreversible|2002|Noé's controversial revenge thriller told in reverse chronological order with disorienting camera work|Prime Beyond the Black Rainbow|2010|Retro-futuristic psychedelic horror about a woman trapped in a mysterious institute|Tubi

The film's exploration of death draws fascinating parallels with other metaphysical journey films like 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) and The Tree of Life (2011). Where those films use montage and natural imagery, Noé employs strobing lights, digital effects, and raw sexuality to represent transcendence. The influence of experimental cinema is clear, particularly Wavelength (1967) and Kenneth Anger's Inauguration of the Pleasure Dome (1954) in how they manipulate time and perspective to alter consciousness.

The film's technical innovation in continuous camera movement influenced a wave of immersive cinema, from Birdman (2014) to 1917 (2019). But while those films use long takes to create real-time tension, Enter the Void uses them to dissolve reality entirely. The overhead shots floating through Tokyo's architecture echo Wings of Desire (1987), but with a neon-noir aesthetic that's been widely imitated in films like Only God Forgives (2013) and Midsommar (2019). A Scanner Darkly|2006|Rotoscoped adaptation of Philip K. Dick's drug paranoia novel with reality-bending visuals|Prime Mandy|2018|Psychedelic revenge horror with Nicolas Cage and mind-melting visuals|Shudder The Holy Mountain|1973|Alejandro Jodorowsky's surreal mystical journey filled with psychedelic imagery|Criterion SUBHEAD: Technical Innovation and Visual Legacy

The film's revolutionary approach to depicting subjective experience has influenced music videos, commercials, and virtual reality experiences. Its seamless transitions between perspectives - from first-person to out-of-body to memory - created new possibilities for visual storytelling. Later films like Doctor Strange (2016) and Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse (2018) borrowed from its psychedelic vocabulary, while maintaining more conventional narratives.
